blocks.text: Therefore, since קפוז kippoz has hitherto been sought in vain both among the birds and among the quadrupeds, let the learned judge whether it does not rather belong to the serpents, among which is the acontias or iaculus, so called διὰ τὸ ὁρμᾶν ὥσπερ τὰ ἀκόντια [dia to horman hōsper ta akontia], because it rushes forward like javelins. So the Scholiast on Nicander. Not very differently Aelian, book 6, ch. 18: Ἤδη δὲ καὶ ἀκοντίων δίκην ἑαυτόν τις μεθίησι, καὶ ἐπιφέρεται. καὶ τὸ ὄνομα ἐξ οὗ δρᾷ ἔχει· κέκληται γὰρ Ἀκοντίας [Ēdē de kai akontiōn dikēn heauton tis methiēsi, kai epipheretai. kai to onoma ex hou dra echei; keklētai gar Akontias]. There is also a certain serpent which launches itself like a javelin (Apostolius ^{i)} reads μεθίστησι [methistēsi], transfers) and rushes upon its prey; and it has its name from what it does, for it is called Iaculus. Accordingly almost all ascribe to it ἅλμα [halma] and προσπήδησιν [prospēdēsin]. Agatharchides, ch. 50, on this kind of serpent: Τὴν πληγὴν δὲ δίδωσι παλλόμενον εἰς ὕψος [Tēn plēgēn de didōsi pallomenon eis hypsos]; It strikes its blow when hurled aloft. This can be accepted. Yet later writers consistently write ἁλλόμενον [hallomenon]. Artemidorus in Strabo, book 16: Ὄφεις δὲ σπιθαμιαῖοι, φοινικοὶ τὴν χρόαν, προσαλλόμενοι [Opheis de spithamiaioi, phoinikoi tēn chroan, prosallomenoi], etc. There are serpents three palms long, of a scarlet colour, leaping at one, etc. Diodorus, book 3, p. 126: Δάκνουσι δὲ προσπηδῶντες, καὶ ἁλλόμενοι πρὸς ὕψος [Daknousi de prospēdōntes, kai hallomenoi pros hypsos]; They bite, springing forward and leaping aloft. Aelian, History, book 8, ch. 13: Ἔστι ἁλτικὸν θηρίον, καὶ διαπηδῆσαι καὶ εἴκοσιν εἰ δέοι, πήχεις οἷόν τε [Esti haltikon thērion, kai diapēdēsai kai eikosin ei deoi, pēcheis hoion te]; It is a serpent strong at leaping, and able, if need be, to leap across a distance of twenty cubits. Galen, ch. 8 of To Piso: Ὁ [III, 199] δὲ ἀκοντίας, ἐκτείνας ἑαυτὸν πάνυ, καὶ ὥς πέρ τι ἀκόντιον ἐφαλλόμενος τοῖς [col. 412] σώμασιν [Ho de akontias, ekteinas heauton pany, kai hōs per ti akontion ephallomenos tois sōmasin]; The iaculus, stretching itself out greatly and leaping upon bodies like a javelin. Isidore, Etymologies, book 12, ch. 4: They leap up into trees, and when some animal comes their way, they throw themselves upon it. And Avicenna ^{k)}, vol. 2, p. 139: ربما كمنت علي الاشجار راصدة وترمي بانفسها علي من يمر بها وتثب منزجة اليه [rubbamā kamanat ʿalī al-ashjār rāṣidatan wa-tarmī bi-anfusihā ʿalī man yamurru bihā wa-tathibu manzajatan ilayhi] Sometimes it lies in ambush up in trees; and if anyone passes near them, it hurls itself and, leaping down, rushes upon him. Hence it is that the acontias is called in Arabic by Avicenna قفازة [qaffāza] kipphaza and طفارة [ṭaffāra] tipphara, as if you were to say the one that leaps at and the one that leaps down. For قفازة [qaffāza] kipphaza is properly said when it strives upward, say from the ground into trees; and طفارة [ṭaffāra] tipphara when it leaps down from on high, say from the trees onto travellers. The former name is formed entirely after the pattern of the Hebrew קפוז kippoz, or kipphoz, as it is certain the ancients read and pronounced it. The radical letters are the same in both, and the form of the noun nearly the same, so far as the difference of the languages allowed. Only in the Arabic قفازة [qaffāza] kipphaza a feminine ending has been added, which is lacking in the noun קפוז kippoz, as the four feminine verbs joined to it show. The ending differs, however, because the Hebrew word for serpent, נחש, is masculine, and the Arabic حية [ḥayya] feminine ^{(4)}.

So much for the word. As for the thing: among the plagues of Africa none is worse than this serpent. Aëtius, in the place cited above, ch. 27: From its bite follow all the things said of the viper, and even worse ones. Avicenna: From its bite there arise violent pain and a hot ulcer over the whole body, and from it death. And Agatharchides, Diodorus and Strabo write that its bite is ἀνίατον [aniaton] or ἀνήκεστον [anēkeston], that is, incurable. Accordingly in Agatharchides this kind of serpent is said to be ἰωδέστατον πάντων [iōdestaton pantōn], the most poisonous of all. For he seems to have written thus, not ἰδιώτατον [idiōtaton], as our editions have it. Nor can this missile be avoided, since it bursts from ambush with such force that it outstrips all flight. It flies as if from a missile-engine, [III, 200] says Pliny; and Solinus says that, whirled from the trees with the greatest force, it pierces whatever animal fortune has put in its way. And Aelian: Ἁλλόμενον δὲ παραχρῆμα ἐνέφυ [Hallomenon de parachrēma enephy], Leaping, it clings at once, namely to whatever it attacks with its leap. Such headlong speed is described thus by Lucan, book 9, line 822.

Behold! far off, from the wood of a barren trunk, a savage serpent (Africa calls it the iaculus) twisted and hurled itself, and passed through the head and pierced temples of Paulus. No poison does its work there; death seized him with the wound. Then it was found how slowly the stones that the sling whirls fly, how sluggishly the air hisses with the Scythian arrow.
